articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: Stanbic Bank Zimbabwe launches awards to reward SMEs
more.description: Business Reporter STANBIC Bank Zimbabwe has launched ‘The Standard Bank Africa Business Awards’ aimed at celebrating and recognising exceptional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across Africa. The Standard Bank Africa Business Awards are the first of their kind and seek to play a pivotal role in driving innovation, resilience, leadership and economic impact within industries and communities. Stanbic Bank head of business and commercial banking, Mr Patson Mahatchi, said the awards are open to eligible SMEs across Africa, including businesses that do not currently bank with Standard Bank Group or Stanbic Bank. Mr Mahatchi said the awards have been established to celebrate and recognise impactful businesses driving growth, innovation and excellence across the continent. The awards feature five categories designed to recognise excellence across key sectors and business segments, including: agriculture; construction; Fast Moving Consumer Goods and retail, manufacturing, women in business and youth-owned businesses. Mr Mahatchi said Stanbic Bank was honoured to celebrate the entrepreneurs, innovators, and business leaders who are shaping Zimbabwe’s economy and contributing to Africa’s growth story through the awards. He said Stanbic Bank is cognizant of the fact that small and medium-sized enterprises across Zimbabwe are creating jobs, developing innovative solutions, strengthening communities, and unlocking opportunities that drive sustainable economic growth. “At Stanbic Bank, we firmly believe that SMEs are the engine of economic development. Driven by our purpose; ‘Zimbabwe is Our Home, We Drive Her Growth’, we continue to support businesses with access to financial solutions, advisory services, market opportunities, and platforms that enable growth,” he said. Mr Mahatchi said The Africa Business Awards also seek to recognise and celebrate those businesses that demonstrate excellence, innovation, growth, and positive social impact. More importantly, these awards provide an opportunity for Zimbabwean businesses to gain continental recognition and showcase their achievements on a larger African stage. He said Stanbic Bank recognizes that extraordinary businesses already exist within Zimbabwe and that their stories deserve to be told. Their achievements deserve to be celebrated while their contribution to economic transformation deserve recognition. “We, therefore, encourage businesses from across Zimbabwe, regardless of size or sector, to participate in these awards,” said Mr Mahatchi, adding that participants can be drawn from those SMEs who would have pioneered innovation, expanded exports, empowered communities, embraced sustainability, or created employment among many others. He said Stanbic Bank Zimbabwe’s commitment extends beyond banking adding that the institution is committed to enabling growth, fostering entrepreneurship, and supporting the ambitions of businesses that will define Africa’s future. “These awards reflect that commitment. To all entrepreneurs and business owners, I encourage you to seize this opportunity, share your story, celebrate your achievements and inspire others. “Let Zimbabwe’s business excellence be represented among the very best on the continent,” said Mr Mahatchi. Stanbic Bank Zimbabwe head of enterprise banking, Sarah Charangwa said the awards are open to registered SMEs operating within eligible African markets where Standard Bank or Stanbic Bank has a presence. The group operates in 21 sub-Saharan African countries, including its anchor market of South Africa, plus countries such Angola, Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe. She said SMEs may enter multiple categories, provided that each submission is completed separately and meets the specific criteria for the relevant category. Businesses may enter the category that best aligns with their core business activities and demonstrated impact. Charangwa said entries will be assessed against criteria including: leadership and vision; innovation and creativity; sustainability and resilience; market and community impact; business growth and scalability as well as financial performance. “Entries will be reviewed by an independent panel comprising business leaders, industry experts, entrepreneurs and representatives from Standard Bank Group and partner organisations. Charangwa said winners stand to receive recognition, networking opportunities, funding, business exposure, mentorship opportunities and other benefits associated with the awards. “Startups may apply provided they are formally registered and able to demonstrate measurable business activity, innovation and growth potential,” she said.

more.title: World First Aid Day widens call to expand life-saving training to grass-root, institutional level
more.description: Sikhulekelani Moyo sikhu.moyo@chronicle.co.zw GOVERNMENT has called for expansion of first-aid training to schools, workplaces, mines, farms and communities, saying widespread life-saving skills can bridge the critical gap between the onset of an emergency and the arrival of professional medical help. Civil Protection Unit (CPU) chief director Mr Nathan Nkomo made the call during the World First Aid Day commemorations hosted by the Zimbabwe Red Cross Society (ZRCS) in Bulawayo on Saturday. He said first aid was particularly important in migration contexts and amid Zimbabwe’s increasingly complex disaster risks, including floods, droughts, cyclones, veld fires, disease outbreaks and road traffic accidents. World First Aid Day highlights the vital role of first aid in bridging the gap between emergencies and professional medical care, especially during the critical first minutes when timely action can save lives,” said Mr Nkomo. People on the move may face injury, illness, trauma, exhaustion, psychosocial distress and barriers to essential services, hence they may require assistance. This year’s theme: “First Aid in Migration Contexts”, focused on the needs of people who are displaced, travelling or returning home. Mr Nkomo cited the recent Government-led repatriation of at least 150 000 Zimbabwean nationals from South Africa as an example of the humanitarian challenges associated with migration. At the Beitbridge Reception Centre, the Zimbabwe Red Cross Society complemented Government efforts by providing bus fares, telephone services, phone-charging facilities and internet connectivity. Mr Nkomo said the interventions were critical in a humanitarian operation of such magnitude, helping returnees reconnect with families, access information, make arrangements for onward travel and restore a sense of dignity. The society's contribution demonstrates that humanitarian assistance goes beyond the provision of food, shelter and medical care. It is also about restoring dignity, facilitating communication, reconnecting families and ensuring that people are able to continue their journey home safely,” he said. With Zimbabwe facing multiple and increasingly interconnected hazards, Mr Nkomo said disaster preparedness must extend beyond Government and emergency services. He said the Zimbabwe Red Cross Society, under the Civil Protection Act, is recognised as an auxiliary to public authorities and sits on the National Civil Protection Committee. Government is also pursuing a new Disaster Risk Management Bill aimed at strengthening coordination in disaster preparedness and response. Mr Nkomo said a whole-of-Government and whole-of-society approach was required, bringing together ministries, departments and agencies, local authorities, security services, humanitarian organisations, the private sector and communities. “Trained first aiders at reception centres, border points, transport hubs and within receiving communities can provide critical lifesaving assistance before professional medical care becomes available. “The migration dimension of first aid must therefore remain central to our national preparedness and response arrangements,” he said. Mr Nkomo called on the Red Cross to continue expanding first-aid training and incorporating it into preparedness exercises at all levels. The call comes as the country seeks to strengthen community resilience against emergencies, with trained first aiders potentially providing immediate assistance before ambulances or other professional responders arrive. Mr Nkomo also commended teams that participated in first-aid demonstrations and competitions during the commemorations, saying the exercises highlighted the importance of continuous practice. The scenarios presented have provided a valuable reminder that emergencies demand more than good intentions. They require people who are trained, confident and able to assess a situation, make the right decisions and provide the correct assistance at the right time, he said. While competitions naturally produce winners, the greatest victory is the collective strengthening of our national capacity to save lives. Mr Nkomo reaffirmed Government’s commitment to working with the Red Cross to strengthen disaster preparedness, anticipatory action and response. As Government, we reaffirm our commitment to working closely with the Society to strengthen national disaster preparedness, anticipatory action and response. As we commemorate World First Aid Day 2026, let us remember that resilience is built before disaster strikes, he said. ZRCS secretary-general Mr Elias Hwenga said their organisation remained committed to expanding first-aid training across the country. The Zimbabwe Red Cross Society has long been at the forefront of providing critical first aid services and training. Our commitment to this cause is unwavering, driven by a deep-seated belief that everyone, regardless of their background, should have access to life-saving knowledge and skills, he said. Mr Hwenga said the migration theme highlighted the need to respond to exhaustion, physical trauma and distress among migrants and displaced people. Our programmes are designed to address the unique challenges and scenarios that arise ensuring that individuals are well-prepared to respond swiftly and effectively to injuries,” he said. In solidarity remarks delivered through an audio message, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies stressed that first aid was rooted in humanity and could be provided by ordinary people when properly trained. Today reminds us of one simple but powerful truth, each and any one of us can save a life, the IFRC representative said. First Aid is the responsibility of everyone, a trained teacher can save a life, a trained student can save a life, a trained kombi driver can also save a life, a trained community volunteer can save a life, a trained migrant can save a life. Every human life has equal value. It does not matter where a person comes from... When someone is injured or in danger, our first response should be compassion. The IFRC urged Zimbabweans who are not trained in first aid to register with the Zimbabwe Red Cross Society. The commemorations began with a march through Bulawayo’s central business district to the ZRCS facility at Makhosi along Lady Stanley Avenue. The programme also featured first-aid competitions involving teams from industry, the private sector, Government and various Red Cross units and services. World First Aid Day is observed annually on the second Saturday of September and was commemorated this year on September 12. The day was established by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies to promote awareness of first aid and its role in saving lives.
